info.title: What are &kexec; and &kdump;, and how do they relate?

abstract.para: &kdump; is built on &kexec;. This section explains how the two relate, how a kernel is loaded with &kexec; and what a captured crash dump contains.

section.title: Why use &kexec;?
section.para: Booting with &kexec; skips the firmware (BIOS/UEFI) initialization stage and the boot loader stage entirely: the currently running kernel loads the new kernel's image directly into memory and jumps to it. Skipping these stages has several practical uses:

listitem.para: Faster reboots. Skipping hardware and firmware re-initialization saves time, which matters if you reboot a system frequently, for example after applying a kernel update.
Avoiding firmware and boot loader problems. Since &kexec; does not depend on a working boot loader configuration, it can boot a system even if the boot loader configuration is broken.

Capturing the state of a crashed kernel. &kdump; uses &kexec; to boot a secondary kernel into a small, pre-reserved area of memory whenever the main kernel panics, so the contents of the main kernel's memory can be saved for analysis before the system reboots normally. Without such a dump, a kernel crash often leaves no record of what went wrong: logging services fail along with the kernel, and the console is frozen or blank.

section.title: Loading a kernel with &kexec;
section.para: The kexec command, which uses the kexec system call, loads a kernel into memory in one of two ways:

listitem.para: Load a kernel into the running system's memory for a regular reboot:

Boot into the loaded kernel later with kexec -e. The command reboots immediately without calling shutdown(8), so services are not stopped cleanly. To load the default kernel, initrd and kernel options from the boot loader configuration instead of naming them yourself, run kexec-bootloader, which is part of the update-bootloader package, and then kexec -e. For routine reboots, systemctl kexec is the simpler choice. See .
Load a kernel into the reserved memory area for use when the system panics:
This kernel starts automatically when the running kernel panics. &kdump; uses this command to load the capture kernel, so you do not normally run it yourself.

section.title: The dual-kernel model
section.para: &kdump; relies on two kernels being involved in a crash:

listitem.para: The production kernel is the kernel that normally runs your system and its workloads.

The capture kernel (also called the crash kernel or &kdump; kernel) is a second, minimal kernel image, together with its own initramfs, loaded ahead of time into a region of memory reserved specifically for it. It stays idle until the production kernel panics. &kdump; builds the initramfs so that it contains the drivers and tools, such as makedumpfile, needed to save the dump.

section.para: When the production kernel panics, it can no longer be trusted to write its own crash information to disk: its data structures may be corrupted, and a normal reboot would overwrite the memory you are trying to inspect. &kexec; solves this by jumping straight from the crashed production kernel into the already-loaded capture kernel, without going through firmware or the boot loader. Because the capture kernel runs from its own reserved memory region, the production kernel's memory contents remain intact and readable while the capture kernel is running.

section.title: What does a captured vmcore file contain?
section.para: Once the capture kernel is running, it writes the production kernel's memory contents to a file called vmcore, together with a copy of the kernel's ring buffer log (dmesg) from the moment of the crash. Depending on how much of memory you choose to include (see and ), a vmcore file can contain:

listitem.para: Kernel state: active kernel data structures, global variables and the call stack that was executing at the moment of the crash.
Process information: the list of processes that were running, along with their individual stacks and registers.
Memory pages: depending on the configured dump level, the actual data held in RAM by the kernel and by user-space applications.

VMCOREINFO: a section that records how the kernel's memory was laid out, such as the kernel release, the page size and the addresses of kernel symbols, so that analysis tools can interpret the raw memory.

section.para: You analyze this file after the system has rebooted, using tools such as crash or GDB. See for details.
